signals.title_or_quote: [P0][Security][Supply Chain] Harden Node/PNPM Build Against Malicious Dependency...
signals.why_relevant: Requests hardening against malicious install scripts in Node/PNPM builds.
signals.drafted_reply: The Rust incident you linked is a good forcing function here. For the PNPM side, beyond --frozen-lockfile you can add a pnpm audit --audit-level=high gate, but that still only catches disclosed CVEs — it would not have caught the event-stream attack until weeks after the malicious version was live. For surfacing transitive dependency changes at PR time (your fourth requirement), diffing the lockfile in CI and piping it through a tool that checks for new install scripts or maintainer handoffs gives you earlier signal than any CVE feed. I built depsentry ({APP_URL}) to do exactly that behavioral check in CI and comment on the PR introducing the risk — free for open-source repos.

rescore.why: The thread is a P0 security issue explicitly focused on hardening against malicious install-time and build-script supply-chain attacks in a Node/PNPM project — exactly the behavioral risk class depsentry addresses.

signals.why_relevant: Seeks to implement supply chain security controls for dependencies.
signals.drafted_reply: The lockfile duplication you flagged is worth fixing first — divergent installs between npm and pnpm can silently introduce different transitive dependency versions, which is exactly the kind of inconsistency supply-chain attackers exploit in the gap between local and CI environments. Once you settle on one lockfile and enforce `npm ci`, adding a CODEOWNERS rule on the lockfile is straightforward and catches human-introduced changes. For provenance beyond that, behavioral signals like new install scripts or maintainer handoffs in minor version bumps are what preceded the event-stream attack and aren't caught by CVE scanners alone. I built depsentry to flag those signals in CI at {APP_URL} — free for open-source repos.

rescore.why: The issue explicitly asks for supply chain hardening including dependency provenance verification and review of new dependencies, which maps directly to what depsentry does.

signals.title_or_quote: Security: Harden CI/CD, Dependencies and Repository Supply Chain
signals.why_relevant: Aims to harden CI/CD and dependencies against supply-chain attacks.
signals.drafted_reply: Your audit checklist covers dependency pinning and vulnerability scanning, but the hardest supply-chain risks — hijacked maintainer accounts, newly added install scripts, obfuscated payloads in minor version bumps — won't show up in CVE feeds until weeks after exposure. For the Node and Python dependency items, it's worth adding behavioral checks: does any package run a postinstall script it didn't before, or did a maintainer change hands recently? Those signals preceded event-stream and similar attacks long before any CVE existed. I built a scanner that catches exactly these behavioral changes in CI and comments on the PR introducing the risk: {APP_URL}.

rescore.why: The issue explicitly lists dependency auditing (Python and Node), supply-chain hardening, and dependency vulnerability scanning as deliverables — exactly what this app addresses.

signals.title_or_quote: How to check if any npm packages are stealing environment variables from my system
signals.why_relevant: Asks about detecting npm packages exfiltrating environment variables.
signals.drafted_reply: Your concern about obfuscated network calls in transitive dependencies is well-founded — the `process.env` exfiltration pattern you described has appeared in real attacks. LavaMoat's compartment approach is the strongest runtime defense here. For pre-install detection, you can also audit packages before they land by checking for newly added network calls in minor version bumps, unexpected postinstall scripts, or recent maintainer changes — these behavioral signals often appear days before any CVE is filed. I built a scanner that watches for exactly those signals in CI: {APP_URL}.

rescore.why: The thread author is directly asking how to detect malicious npm packages exfiltrating env vars through obfuscated code in deep dependencies — exactly the behavioral supply-chain risk depsentry is built to catch.
